recent_posts.author: Jnr6
recent_posts.content_text:
Pocket Node v1.8.5 is out
This release makes the app lock smarter, keeps every wallet syncing when you change sync settings, improves Nervos DAO unlocks, and cleans up a few confusing activity entries.
Unlock returns you where you were. Coming back to the app no longer drops you on Home. A half-typed send or an open transaction is still there after you unlock.
Secrets are cleared when the app locks. A recovery phrase or private key on screen, or being typed, is wiped on every lock.
Restored wallets sync their recent history. Imports now start from Recent (about the last 30 days), and you choose the sync start point after every import.
All your wallets keep syncing. Changing one wallet’s sync mode no longer stops the others.
Nervos DAO improved. Unlock can’t be pressed twice, a claimed deposit no longer comes back as unlockable, and the false “Deep rescan” prompt is gone.
Self Transfer label. Sending to your own address shows “Self Transfer” and only the network fee, not “Sent”.
Network services in Settings. The only two outside services the app uses (fiat price and update checks) are listed, each with its own switch.
Download: Release Pocket Node v1.8.5 · RaheemJnr/pocket-node · GitHub or https://pocket-node.com

Nice M1, the subject lock model is what caught my eye. I’m building CrowdCell (all-or-nothing crowdfunding on CKB, live on testnet), and every campaign already stores its creator’s lock, so readClaims could show a creator’s reputation on the campaign page without asking them to link anything first.
The other direction would be CrowdCell issuing a claim when a campaign gets funded and actually pays out, since that’s a strong signal for someone’s next campaign. Is there a v1 schema that fits something like that, or would a partner register its own? Happy to be an early integration for the partner issuance side.

topics.title: Spark Program | DAO Cycle Alerts: Telegram reminders before your Nervos DAO cycle ends

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | DAO Cycle Alerts: Telegram reminders before your Nervos DAO cycle ends
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @yukikawata,
Thank you for your continued interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the DAO Cycle Alerts proposal.
After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal has been assigned a status of Pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise.
The committee recognizes the practical value of your idea — reminding Nervos DAO depositors when their 180-epoch cycle is about to end is a genuinely useful service, especially for long-term holders who do not check their wallets frequently. The scenario you described (Li’s October purchase) is relatable and well-articulated.
Main Revision Recommendations:
Privacy and security model: Your bot watches CKB addresses and associates them with Telegram chat IDs. This linkage between a real-world identity (Telegram account) and a CKB balance could pose privacy risks — a Telegram handle is often traceable to a person, and now it is paired with their deposit amounts and withdrawal timing. Please clarify: How do you plan to address these privacy concerns? Will you offer any opt-in anonymity features ? How do you handle the risk of a compromised Telegram account exposing a user’s CKB holdings?
Scope and budget adjustment: The committee appreciates the clean, read-only design (no keys, no signatures, public chain data only). However, the current scope — Telegram bot + CLI + npm package + Cloudflare Workers infrastructure — appears broader than necessary for a Spark-level MVP. The committee suggests focusing on the core Telegram bot functionality first. Given the simplicity of the core feature, the committee would offer 100U for this project. Please adjust your budget and scope accordingly.
Use case clarification: The committee considers this a project with clear goals and a sufficiently focused scope. Taking into account its functionality and implementation difficulty, the committee has decided to provide 100 U in support.
Please revise and resubmit based on the feedback above. We will arrange a new round of review as soon as possible.
Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
cc: @zz_tovarishch , @Hanssen , @yixiu.ckbfans.bit

topics.title: Spark Program | Fiber Weir — Condition-Gated Payment Streams for Fiber Network

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Fiber Weir — Condition-Gated Payment Streams for Fiber Network
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @Carl,
The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regrets to Reject Fiber Weir project.
We want to be transparent about the reasoning behind this decision:
Scope Overlap with Existing Ecosystem: The “programmable conditional payment” roadmap item you reference from Fiber Network’s repository is indeed unfinished work by the core team. However, this falls into a category of protocol-level development that the committee views as part of Fiber’s own core roadmap rather than a Spark-appropriate independent implementation. Relatedly, AgentPay—which you correctly identify as an existing application-layer solution using hold-invoice mechanisms—already covers a significant portion of the practical use cases for condition-gated payments. While we recognize your differentiation (on-chain contract conditions vs. secret-knowledge gates), we are not convinced the incremental value over AgentPay’s approach is substantial enough for a standalone grant at this time.
Technical Feasibility Concerns: The proposal requires solving non-trivial challenges around on-chain condition verification and payment channel integration. Specifically, we note the requirement to address how the “on-chain-verifiable condition” would be checked in a channel context—whether this is an on-chain interaction or channel-internal verification is not fully addressed. For a $1,000 budget, we believe the scope of implementing this novel primitive alongside a full test infrastructure is ambitious, and we remain uncertain about the completeness of the deliverable without a clearer technical breakdown.
It should also be noted that, since your deliverables for the Fiber RGB++ Swap project fell far short of the proposal’s requirements, the committee has doubts about your ability and willingness to deliver.
Thank you very much for all the hard work your team has put in. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
cc: @Hanssen @yixiu.ckbfans.bit @zz_tovarishch

topics.title: Spark Program | Spark Verify - Reproducible Acceptance Checks for CKB Projects

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Spark Verify - Reproducible Acceptance Checks for CKB Projects
recent_posts.author: Akane
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @zz_tovarishch,
Thanks for the thoughtful questions, and sorry this reply took a while. I wanted to come back with something you could actually inspect and run, rather than another plan.
For the Week 5 example, I chose HNO3Miracle/CKB-UGMP at revision 543def6e717b2d67f619a76c3d9283e55b211b83, focusing on its CCC-based Spore mint path. I built a bounded adaptation on a fresh local OffCKB devnet: ckb-verify submits the signed transaction, then records the committed result and resulting Spore Cell. It is public in PR #7 at commit a756291, with all three CI jobs passing.
I want to be careful about what this proves. It does not cover the browser UI, wallet connection, Pinata, hosted RPC, or public testnet, and it does not imply validation of the whole DApp or endorsement from its maintainer. It is a practical feasibility test.
The evidence format is now straightforward:
verify.toml describes the setup, transaction-producing steps, and expected outcomes.
report.json records the expected and observed results, rejection details, provenance, and outcome/environment digests.
Terminal and CI output give reviewers a short human-readable summary.
I also added a line-by-line manifest guide, a report guide, and a checked report from a real fresh-OffCKB run. I am keeping v0.1 focused, so I am not proposing a hosted dashboard.
I took the naming suggestion and adopted ckb-verify for the CLI and future package. The current public main is still an unreleased 0.0.1 technical preview, not grant completion. Work already completed is priced at $0; the remaining $1,000 covers only unfinished v0.1 work and an external pilot or documented no-go result.
Thanks again for pushing me to make this concrete. I hope this gives the committee what it needs to resume the review.

recent_posts.topic_title: Introducing CKB Kickstarter: Decentralized All-or-Nothing Crowdfunding on Nervos CKB (Testnet MVP Live)
recent_posts.author: Ayoub_Lesfer
recent_posts.content_text:
Update: v1.2 is live on testnet, and the project is now CrowdCell
It’s been a while since the last update here, so here’s where things are.
What changed since May
Finalization is trustless now. The campaign cell keeps the running total on-chain and every pledge updates it. The script checks Funded or Unsuccessful against that total, so it doesn’t matter who triggers finalization, the bot or anyone else. That closes the gap Arthur pointed out.
Anyone can settle. Release to the creator, refunds to backers and the ~180 day fail-safe can all be triggered by anyone, and the funds can only go where the rules say.
All of Officeyutong’s review findings are fixed, including the two high ones (the fail-safe backdoor and the receipt/refund mismatch).
An exact balance accounting test caught 4 fund-routing bugs before testnet (fake pledge amounts, a release double count, a merge amount rewrite, and destroying a campaign without paying out). All fixed. Backers also get their storage deposits back now.
Pledges under load: 3 simultaneous pledges to the same campaign all land now, before only 1 did.
CrowdCell
New name, and a landing page that explains how pledges settle and exactly who can do what, checked against the contracts: https://crowdcell.vercel.app
landing-dark1920×1080 153 KB
Short video of the flow:
https://x.com/crowdcellckb/status/2105250207470641472
Fees
@RetricSu thanks again for the input in May. The 5% success-only fee design is still the plan, but it moved to the mainnet phase. Fees only matter once real money moves, and that code should go through the audit first.
Next
I’m planning to bring the grant proposal back next week, scoped down to testnet productisation (~$5k). Mainnet and the audit would be a separate proposal later. Feedback is welcome before then, especially anything that would stop you from running a real campaign on it.
You can try it on testnet with JoyID. Test CKB is free from the faucet.

topics.title: Post-quantum ownership on CKB without changing your contract: notes from Cells

recent_posts.topic_title: Post-quantum ownership on CKB without changing your contract: notes from Cells
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
Any CKB contract that authorises an owner by lock hash, and accepts any lock there, can have post-quantum owners today with no contract change. The stored owner only has to be the hash of a lock under Nervos’s quantum-resistant lock script, which verifies SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+, NIST FIPS 205) signatures.
We build Cells, a naming protocol on CKB, and did this there: .cell names on mainnet can be owned this way since September 2026. These are our notes: why it works, what we checked about the lock, what the chain refused when we attacked it, and two things we learned about CCC on the way.
quantum-ownership-diagram2800×1800 294 KB
Why it needs no contract change
A type script that checks ownership this way never verifies a signature itself. It stores the owner as a lock hash, and accepts an owner action when the same transaction spends a cell under that lock. Whether the lock runs secp256k1, a multisig or SPHINCS+ is the lock’s business. Moving an owner to a post-quantum key is therefore an ordinary transfer, to an address under the SPHINCS+ lock.
In Cells the check is require_owner: a name’s cell stores the first 20 bytes of its owner’s lock hash, and the transaction must spend a cell whose lock hash starts with them, under a lock that needs its holder to sign. The deployed code is that published source; cellula.id/api/verify compares the code cells on mainnet with the hashes a reproducible build gives, and answers verified: true.
The lock, checked
Before pointing anyone at it, we checked the mainnet deployment of c-sphincs-all-in-one-lock against upstream and against the chain. Cells uses the SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s parameter set. Each line names what it was checked against.
Value
Checked against
Standard
NIST FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA); one lock serves all 12 parameter sets
upstream README
Parameter set
SHA2-128s: 32-byte public key, 7,856-byte signature
the SDK’s constants; a test signature made and verified with @noble/post-quantum
args
blake2b-256, personalization ckb-sphincs+-sct, over 80 01 01 01 62 and the public key
upstream format notes; the SDK
Witness lock
7,893 bytes: prefix 80 01 01 01 63, public key, signature

A type script that checks ownership this way never verifies a signature itself. topics.title: Spark Program | LiquidLane: Fiber Receive Capacity Marketplace | RESUBMISSION

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | LiquidLane: Fiber Receive Capacity Marketplace | RESUBMISSION
recent_posts.author: Fidelcoder
recent_posts.content_text:
1. Project Overview
LiquidLane is a CKB-native marketplace where merchants and applications obtain Fiber receive capacity from independent node operators. Providers publish capacity and opening fees, fund channels from their own wallets, and retain their keys. Merchants choose an offer, verify delivery, and pay the provider directly.
The product brings provider discovery, channel provisioning, delivery verification, and fee tracking into one workflow.
2. Team Profile
FidelCoder — Developer and maintainer. Responsible for LiquidLane’s Rust backend, local connector, and Next.js application, with hands-on experience building CKB transaction flows, JoyID authentication, and Fiber channel integrations.
Contact Details
GitHub: FidelCoder (Fidel) · GitHub
Core repository: GitHub - FidelCoder/liquidlane-core: Backend service for vault accounting, liquidity requests, Fiber channel deployment, and fee distribution on LiquidLane. · GitHub
App repository: GitHub - FidelCoder/liquidlane-app: Web app for managing stablecoin liquidity vaults, channel capacity requests, and LP yield on LiquidLane. · GitHub
Web interface: https://liquidlane-app.vercel.app
Initial Proposal: LiquidLane: LP-Backed Fiber Channel Liquidity
3. Project Background
A working wallet or checkout does not automatically mean a merchant can receive Fiber payments. Receiving requires sufficient channel capacity funded by peers toward the merchant. CKB held in the merchant’s own wallet does not, by itself, provide that capacity. An application can therefore be correctly integrated while customer payments still fail because the receiving path lacks liquidity.
This creates a coordination problem on both sides. Merchants and application developers need to find funded peers, compare terms, and establish when receiving capacity is usable. Node operators need a way to advertise available capital, set prices and funding limits, and reach customers who need it.
Channel creation provides the underlying mechanism. A usable capacity market also needs discovery, clear service terms, delivery evidence, and payment records. LiquidLane brings those pieces together so acquiring receive capacity becomes a repeatable service for CKB wallets, merchant tools, and payment applications.
4. Solution
LiquidLane makes a defined amount of usable receive capacity available as a priced service. Providers publish how much they can supply and the opening fee they charge. Merchants can compare offers, understand the capital required by their receiving node, and choose terms suited to their payment needs.
Each purchase has an agreement signed by both parties, binding the participants, capacity, funding amount, fee recipient, and opening deadline. A local connector enforces the provider’s funding limits before committing capital. This makes provisioning repeatable while keeping spending authority with the node operator.
Delivery checks combine committed channel funding, matching observations from both nodes, and a paid test invoice. The agreed capacity must remain available after the test payment. A signed receipt records the agreement and delivery evidence, while fee tracking distinguishes paid, outstanding, and waived amounts.
Supply comes from operators committing their own capital to native bidirectional channels. They set their prices and earn opening fees and any routing fees actually received. Merchants pay for receiving capability and retain their incoming payments. LiquidLane gives these parties a common service agreement and operational record while native Fiber handles payment routing and settlement.
5. Technical Approach
The system combines a Rust/Axum coordinator, SQLite persistence, a local Rust connector, and a Next.js/TypeScript interface with JoyID signing. The release targets native CKB on testnet and Fiber 0.9.0.
Fund control: the coordinator holds no participant signing keys. Each connector independently checks signatures, funding limits, peer identity, and agreed fees. The node negotiates native channel funding and supplies its own closing destination. Funding and settlement use Fiber’s native CKB scripts.
Capacity accounting: a 500 CKB offer requires a 600 CKB provider contribution: 500 usable capacity, 99 native reserve, and 1 for the delivery probe. The merchant funds its own reserve, and both wallets need transaction headroom. These amounts are itemized before acceptance.
Payments and recovery: customer payments move through native Fiber channels. The provider receives corresponding value in its incoming channel; the merchant owns received payments. Existing payments and native closure remain available if the coordinator stops. Recovery follows Fiber’s settlement rules and delays, with confirmed wallet outputs checked separately from channel status.
Service boundaries: this product sells initial capacity. It does not guarantee duration or replenishment. Fees follow delivery and can remain unpaid; local limits bound provider exposure. Participants remain responsible for securing their node keys and current channel state.
6. To-Do List
Milestone 1 — Marketplace and onboarding improvements · Weeks 1–2
Week 1: package connector releases with checksums and installation instructions; add setup diagnostics for pairing, connectivity, service startup, and funding readiness.
Week 2: add offer filtering by capacity, fee, and availability; implement offer renewal while preserving accepted quotes; improve mobile onboarding.
Completion: an operator can install the packaged connector, diagnose setup problems, and publish or renew an offer. A merchant can find a suitable provider through the improved interface.
Milestone 2 — Reliability and beta release · Weeks 3–4
Week 3: add actionable recovery guidance for interrupted setup, uncertain payments, and pending settlement; introduce order/fee activity exports and activation metrics.
Week 4: automate coordinator backups and verify restoration; restore hosted API connectivity and persistent storage; test machine reboot, fresh-node JoyID funding, and interruption recovery.
Completion: publish a usable testnet release with working hosted services, documented recovery procedures, and passing checks that retries do not duplicate funding or payments. The market beta begins after this milestone.
Milestone 3 — Market beta and product iteration · Weeks 5–6
Week 5: recruit 30–40 beta participants through Nervos/Fiber communities and direct outreach to operators, merchants, and wallet/application builders. Target at least three independently operated providers.
Week 6: address beta defects, refine onboarding, and publish results covering usability, transaction completion, provider economics, and repeat-use interest.
Completion targets: 30–40 participants completing a role-specific workflow and feedback; at least ten completed capacity purchases across independent providers; a released update addressing reported issues. Report registrations, active participants, completed purchases, and failed or unpaid orders separately.
7. Required Funding & Funding Breakdown
Total requested: $1,000 USD.
Milestone 1 — $350: $300 for onboarding and marketplace development; $50 for connector packaging and installation documentation.
Milestone 2 — $350: $250 for reliability improvements and recovery testing; $100 for hosting, domain, and monitoring.
Milestone 3 — $300: $100 for recruitment and onboarding support; $100 for structured usability sessions and feedback collection; $100 for product fixes and the completion report.
Funding supports development, deployment, and participant testing. Node capital remains participant-controlled. An external security audit and mainnet deployment are outside this scope.
8. Deliverables + How to Verify
M1: packaged connector and improved marketplace. Install the published release on Linux x86_64, follow the setup guide, publish/renew an offer, and filter available capacity. Provide binaries, checksums, source changes, and a short walkthrough.
M2: hosted testnet release and recovery package. Open the app and health endpoint, complete a purchase, and inspect its funding, probe, and fee evidence. Publish restart, backup/restore, and payment-retry results with expected outputs.
M3: beta release and results report. Publish participant totals, completed workflows, transaction references, feedback, costs, and resolved issues. Count participants once; project-operated nodes do not count as independent providers.
Reviewers can inspect recordings, receipts, and explorer links without running nodes. Live reproduction requires compatible Fiber nodes, a CKB RPC/indexer, testnet funds, and a separate payer route. Build instructions specify Rust 1.91 and Node 22.
Verification guides:
Connector setup: liquidlane-core/docs/automatic-provider-setup.md at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub
Operations and recovery: liquidlane-core/docs/marketplace-operations.md at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub
9. Current State vs. Funded Work
Already implemented: wallet authentication, node pairing, signed quotes, local funding limits, durable orders, automatic channel opening, delivery checks, direct fees, and merchant/provider interfaces. Both repositories use the MIT license.
Demonstrated: automatic delivery of 500 CKB, a routed probe, a confirmed opening fee, one real JoyID purchase, and outage/recovery verification. These used project-operated nodes. The normal Rust suite passes 88 tests, with two additional tests ignored.
Evidence:
Automatic capacity delivery: liquidlane-core/docs/evidence/automatic-capacity at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub
Provider funding: liquidlane-core/docs/evidence/provider-funding at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub
Payments during coordinator outage: liquidlane-core/docs/evidence/coordinator-outage at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub
Settlement and service recovery: liquidlane-core/docs/evidence/settlement-recovery at main · FidelCoder/liquidlane-core · GitHub
Funded additions: packaged connector distribution, setup diagnostics, offer filtering/renewal, recovery guidance, activity exports, automated backups, and hosted-release improvements, followed by the participant testing specified in Milestone 3. Hosted API restoration, full reboot testing, and JoyID funding of a newly managed node remain pending.
10. CKB Alignment
LiquidLane connects Fiber’s native channels with CKB settlement and JoyID wallet signing. Its open-source connector, marketplace API, and delivery receipts give CKB developers reusable components for acquiring receive capacity. This supports wallet and checkout integrations while keeping channel operation and capital under participant control

Delivery checks combine committed channel funding, matching observations from both nodes, and a paid test invoice. The agreed capacity must remain available after the test payment. A signed receipt records the agreement and delivery evidence, while fee tracking distinguishes paid, outstanding, and waived amounts.

Supply comes from operators committing their own capital to native bidirectional channels. They set their prices and earn opening fees and any routing fees actually received. Merchants pay for receiving capability and retain their incoming payments. LiquidLane gives these parties a common service agreement and operational record while native Fiber handles payment routing and settlement.

5. Technical Approach

The system combines a Rust/Axum coordinator, SQLite persistence, a local Rust connector, and a Next.js/TypeScript interface with JoyID signing. The release targets native CKB on testnet and Fiber 0.9.0.

Fund control: the coordinator holds no participant signing keys. Each connector independently checks signatures, funding limits, peer identity, and agreed fees. The node negotiates native channel funding and supplies its own closing destination. Funding and settlement use Fiber’s native CKB scripts.

Capacity accounting: a 500 CKB offer requires a 600 CKB provider contribution: 500 usable capacity, 99 native reserve, and 1 for the delivery probe. The merchant funds its own reserve, and both wallets need transaction headroom. These amounts are itemized before acceptance.

Payments and recovery: customer payments move through native Fiber channels. The provider receives corresponding value in its incoming channel; the merchant owns received payments. Existing payments and native closure remain available if the coordinator stops. Recovery follows Fiber’s settlement rules and delays, with confirmed wallet outputs checked separately from channel status.

Service boundaries: this product sells initial capacity. It does not guarantee duration or replenishment. Fees follow delivery and can remain unpaid; local limits bound provider exposure. Participants remain responsible for securing their node keys and current channel state.

10. CKB Alignment

LiquidLane connects Fiber’s native channels with CKB settlement and JoyID wallet signing. Its open-source connector, marketplace API, and delivery receipts give CKB developers reusable components for acquiring receive capacity. This supports wallet and checkout integrations while keeping channel operation and capital under participant control
